title: Right triangles and trigonometry
what_is_tested: These questions use the Pythagorean theorem, the special right triangles (\(45^{\circ}\)-\(45^{\circ}\)-\(90^{\circ}\) and \(30^{\circ}\)-\(60^{\circ}\)-\(90^{\circ}\)) and the ratios sine, cosine and tangent to find missing sides or angles. Harder ones use the fact that \(\sin x^{\circ} = \cos(90 - x)^{\circ}\), model a context such as an angle of elevation, or find a ratio from partial information.
how_to_spot: A right triangle (marked with a small square or described in words) with two sides, or a side and an angle, given; or any \(\sin\), \(\cos\) or \(\tan\) in the question; or a context with a slope, ramp, ladder or angle of elevation.
method: Find the right angle; the side across from it is the hypotenuse, the longest side.
Label the other two sides opposite and adjacent, relative to the angle in the question.
Choose the tool: the Pythagorean theorem for three sides; a special right triangle for \(30^{\circ}\), \(45^{\circ}\) or \(60^{\circ}\) (both are on the reference sheet); SOH-CAH-TOA otherwise.
Set up the equation and solve; if only a ratio is known, write the sides as multiples of \(k\).
Check: the hypotenuse is the longest side, and every sine or cosine of an acute angle is between 0 and 1.
pitfalls: Labeling opposite and adjacent from the wrong angle, which turns \(\cos B\) into \(\cos A\) (wrong_quantity).
Inverting a ratio, for example taking \(\tan A\) as adjacent over opposite (reciprocal).
Adding the legs instead of their squares in \(a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}\), or forgetting the final square root (wrong_formula).
Putting \(x\sqrt{3}\) across from the \(30^{\circ}\) angle; the shortest side is across from \(30^{\circ}\) (concept).
Leaving the calculator in Rad mode when the angles are in degrees (arithmetic).
calculator: Use the Scientific tab for angles that are not special, such as \(40^{\circ}\): check that it is set to Deg, then evaluate \(\sin\), \(\cos\) or \(\tan\) directly. For \(30^{\circ}\), \(45^{\circ}\) and \(60^{\circ}\), the exact side patterns are faster and match answer choices written with radicals.

cards.title: Foundations: Pythagoras and SOH-CAH-TOA
steps: Mark the right angle and the hypotenuse across from it.
From the angle in the question, label the opposite side and the adjacent side.
Write the ratio (sine = opposite over hypotenuse, cosine = adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent = opposite over adjacent) or \(a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}\).
Substitute the side lengths and simplify.

worked_example.stem: In right triangle \(PQR\), what is the value of \(\tan P\)?
walkthrough: The right angle is at \(Q\), so the hypotenuse is \(\overline{PR} = 29\).
From angle \(P\), the opposite side is \(\overline{QR} = 21\) and the adjacent side is \(\overline{PQ} = 20\).
Tangent is opposite over adjacent: \(\tan P = \frac{21}{20}\), choice D.
Choice C, \(\frac{20}{21}\), is the reciprocal (adjacent over opposite), and choice B, \(\frac{21}{29}\), is \(\sin P\). Quick check of the labels: \(20^{2} + 21^{2} = 841 = 29^{2}\).
worked_example.verify:
P=figure['points']
d=lambda a,b: sqrt((P[a][0]-P[b][0])**2+(P[a][1]-P[b][1])**2)
ang=lambda a,v,b: N(acos(((P[a][0]-P[v][0])*(P[b][0]-P[v][0])+(P[a][1]-P[v][1])*(P[b][1]-P[v][1]))/(d(a,v)*d(b,v)))*180/pi)
assert P['Q'][0]==P['R'][0] and P['Q'][1]==P['P'][1]
opp=d('Q','R'); adj=d('P','Q'); hyp=d('P','R')
assert opp==21 and adj==20 and hyp==29
ans=opp/adj
assert value(choices[answer])==ans
assert all(value(choices[c])!=ans for c in choices if c!=answer)
assert value(choices['C'])==1/ans and value(choices['B'])==opp/hyp

cards.title: Medium: special right triangles and complements
steps: Spot a \(30^{\circ}\), \(45^{\circ}\) or \(60^{\circ}\) angle, or a square or equilateral triangle that splits into one.
Write the side pattern from the reference sheet: \(s, s, s\sqrt{2}\) or \(x, x\sqrt{3}, 2x\).
Find the multiplier from the side you know, then the side you need; for complementary angles use \(\sin x^{\circ} = \cos(90 - x)^{\circ}\).
Answer the question asked (a perimeter, a height) and check that the hypotenuse is the longest side.

worked_example.stem: The playing surface of a carrom board is a square. The diagonal of the playing surface is \(74\sqrt{2}\) centimeters long. What is the perimeter, in centimeters, of the playing surface?
walkthrough: The diagonal cuts the square into two \(45^{\circ}\)-\(45^{\circ}\)-\(90^{\circ}\) triangles, and the diagonal is their hypotenuse.
The reference sheet gives the sides of that triangle as \(s, s, s\sqrt{2}\). So \(s\sqrt{2} = 74\sqrt{2}\), and \(s = 74\).
Stopping at \(s = 74\) answers a different question, and \(4 \cdot 74\sqrt{2}\) wrongly uses the diagonal as a side.
worked_example.verify:
s=symbols('s',positive=True)
ss=solve(Eq(s*sqrt(2),74*sqrt(2)),s)[0]
P=figure['points']
assert P['B'][0]-P['A'][0]==ss and P['C'][1]-P['B'][1]==ss and P['D'][1]-P['A'][1]==ss
assert Rational(spr_answers[0])==4*ss==296

cards.title: Advanced: trigonometry in context, with the calculator
steps: Draw the right triangle the context describes and mark the known angle and side.
Pick the ratio that links the side you know and the side you want, relative to that angle.
Solve for the unknown (for example, height \(= 30\tan 40^{\circ}\)); evaluate in the Scientific tab set to Deg, or use exact values for special angles.
Add any extra pieces the context includes (an eye or instrument height), then round as the question says.

worked_example.stem: A surveyor sets up an instrument on level ground 30 meters from the base of a vertical tower. The instrument's lens is 1.4 meters above the ground, and the angle of elevation from the lens to the top of the tower is \(40^{\circ}\), as shown. To the nearest tenth of a meter, what is the height of the tower?
walkthrough: The right triangle has vertices at the lens \(L\), the point \(Q\) on the tower at lens height, and the top \(T\). Its horizontal leg is \(LQ = 30\) meters, and the angle at \(L\) is \(40^{\circ}\).
\(QT\) is opposite the \(40^{\circ}\) angle and \(LQ\) is adjacent, so use tangent: \(\tan 40^{\circ} = \frac{QT}{30}\), which gives \(QT = 30\tan 40^{\circ}\).
In the Scientific tab, set to Deg, \(30\tan 40^{\circ} \approx 25.17\) meters.
Add the lens height: \(25.17 + 1.4 = 26.57\), which rounds to 26.6. Enter 26.6.
Forgetting the 1.4 meters gives 25.2. A negative result means the calculator was in Rad mode.
worked_example.verify:
P=figure['points']
d=lambda a,b: sqrt((P[a][0]-P[b][0])**2+(P[a][1]-P[b][1])**2)
ang=lambda a,v,b: N(acos(((P[a][0]-P[v][0])*(P[b][0]-P[v][0])+(P[a][1]-P[v][1])*(P[b][1]-P[v][1]))/(d(a,v)*d(b,v)))*180/pi)
h=Rational('1.4')+30*tan(40*pi/180)
assert abs(N(h)-Rational(spr_answers[0]))<0.05 and Rational(spr_answers[0])==Rational('26.6')
assert P['Q'][0]-P['L'][0]==30 and P['L'][0]==P['G'][0] and P['Q'][0]==P['F'][0]==P['T'][0]
assert abs(P['L'][1]-1.4)<1e-9 and abs(P['T'][1]-N(h))<0.01 and abs(ang('Q','L','T')-40)<0.1
assert abs(N(h-Rational('1.4'))-Rational('25.2'))<0.05

cards.title: Challenge: ratios with a multiplier
steps: Turn the given ratio (or a cofunction fact) into side lengths with a multiplier: \(\tan A = \frac{12}{5}\) means sides \(12k\) and \(5k\).
Use the Pythagorean theorem to write the third side in terms of \(k\); in a triangle without a right angle, draw an altitude first.
Use the extra fact (a perimeter, an area, one actual side) to find \(k\).
Compute the requested side or ratio and check it against the original ratio.

worked_example.stem: In right triangle \(ABC\), angle \(C\) is a right angle, \(\tan A = 2.4\), and the perimeter of the triangle is 60. What is the length of \(\overline{AC}\)?
walkthrough: \(\tan A = 2.4 = \frac{12}{5}\), so the leg opposite angle \(A\) is \(BC = 12k\) and the adjacent leg is \(AC = 5k\) for some \(k > 0\).
Choice D, 24, is \(BC\), the leg opposite angle \(A\), not the adjacent leg; choices B and C use the ratio numbers 12 and 13 without finding \(k\).
worked_example.verify:
k=symbols('k',positive=True)
ks=solve(Eq(12*k+5*k+sqrt((12*k)**2+(5*k)**2),60),k)
assert ks==[2] and Rational('2.4')==Rational(12,5)
ans=5*ks[0]
assert Rational(12*ks[0],ans)==Rational('2.4')
assert value(choices[answer])==ans==10
assert all(value(choices[c])!=ans for c in choices if c!=answer)
assert value(choices['D'])==12*ks[0]
